g.passage: Gdansk in late October smells of wet grass and diesel from the shipyards, and that is where Milena found me, sitting on the bench beside the soccer field my brothers used to rule every evening. She had known my parents since before I was born, and she still called me Ksenia the goalkeeper. Our house two streets away was empty except for one thing: the cracked leather ball my father had signed for each of us. I told Milena I would throw it out, because keeping it felt like refusing to leave. She said nothing. She kicked it once across the darkening grass and waited. I ran after it before I knew I had decided to, and somewhere near the far goal I understood that a thing could be carried forward without becoming a weight. We walked home under the floodlights, the ball under my arm.

The bride said nothing and rolled the dough again. To the family at the long table outside, the two women looked like a perfectly matched pair. g.passage: Two rules governed the salt flat behind the house I rented outside Port of Spain: never walk on a pan that is still drying, and never rake against the wind. Shanice, my landlord, taught me both in my first month there, though I had only asked her about the leaking roof. She was the last person on that stretch of coast who still harvested salt by hand, and her own children had moved to offices in the city. She called me Alisha-girl, as if I were a niece rather than a tenant. Each evening she handed me the long wooden rake and corrected my wrist without comment. I assumed she simply wanted cheap help.
